english.html: of beard, nevertheless he was recognised by all, and singularly by the said Pierre Guerre his uncle, who had received and made much of him as his nephew: until, looking more closely to his affairs, the defendant wished to recover his said property, and the fruits that had been received from it during his absence; whereof the said Pierre Guerre, the uncle, having often been amicably admonished, had for a long time fed him with fine words.

notes.citation: Cicero, Pro Cluentio (passage not located); Code 8.13 (De pignoribus et hypothecis), l. Debitores (fragment not identified)
notes.original: Ciceron en l'Oraiſon pro Cluentio. l. de bitores. C. de pignor.
notes.gloss: Evidently belongs to the opening sentence on the creditor who admonishes his debtor before suing him.

notes.citation: Digest 13.7.4 (De pigneraticia actione, l. Si convenit, cited as Si convenerit)
notes.original: l. ſi conuenerit. D. de pi gno. actio.
notes.gloss: Ulpian: a creditor who sells a pledge against agreement is liable for theft, unless he has three times given the debtor notice to pay — the "twice and three times" of the text.

english.html: In former times, when some creditor wished to call his debtor into judgment, before entering into suit he would take him aside, and admonish and call upon him familiarly to pay and satisfy him, not once only, but most often twice and three times. Thus Proculus the Jurisconsult teaches us that, if our neighbour or another does us some wrong, [we ought] to speak to him and amicably represent it to him before bringing him to law. I WISH, says he, that you would speak with Hiberus, so that he may not do an unjust thing <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>. Acts not only humane and full of all civility, but also savouring of Christianity, by whose law we are commanded to correct our neighbour before threatening him <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>, and to take up a quarrel with no one, but to be humane, gracious and charitable, using all gentleness and courtesy toward men <sup class="mk" data-key="e">e</sup>; from whom, if we receive some wrong or injury, we must nevertheless not hold him who offends us as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother <sup class="mk" data-key="f">f</sup>, and reprove and correct him amicably between ourselves and him alone <sup class="mk" data-key="g">g</sup>.

notes.citation: Digest 8.2.13 pr. (De servitutibus praediorum urbanorum, l. Quidam Hiberus)
notes.original: l. quidam Hyberus. D. de ſeruit. vrb: prædio.
notes.gloss: Proculus, on a neighbour Hiberus who built baths against a party wall: "on which matter I wish you to speak with Hiberus, so that he may not do an unlawful thing" (volo cum Hibero loquaris, ne rem illicitam faciat).
Admonish a friend, lest he have done it not; and if he have, that he do it no more.
To speak evil of no man, not to be contentious, but gentle, showing all meekness to all men.

notes.original: ij des Theſ ſaloniciens C. iij.
notes.gloss: Count him not as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.

notes.original: S Mathieu c. xviij. S. Luc c xvij. Leuitique c. xix.
notes.gloss: Go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone; if thy brother trespass, rebuke him; thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour.
